name.text: Ch10 Ten Minutes Away: accounting for journey time

questiontext.text:
A traveller needs to get from somewhere in Nairobi to JKIA airport. How many minutes should they allow for the trip?

With no information at all, the typical trip takes 60 minutes. Six clue cards each tell you something about this particular trip, but you may only turn over two of them.

How to play

  1. Turn over two cards by clicking them. You can't turn them back, so choose the two you think will tell you most.
  2. Work out your prediction using the chart below: start at 60 minutes and add the adjustment for each of your two cards.
  3. Decide how many minutes to allow. The four face-down cards and plain chance can still change the trip, so you may want some spare time.
  4. Press Check. All six cards and the actual journey time are then revealed.

Scoring. Getting to the airport with anything from 0 to 45 minutes to spare is a good result. More than 45 minutes is a long wait, so it gets half marks. Arriving after the time you allowed means a missed flight and no marks.

What a local driver knows

This chart shows how much each clue adds to or takes off the typical 60 minutes. Clues add together. For example, 17:30 on a Friday is \(60 + 20 + 10 = 90\) minutes before you know anything else.

Time of day 05:30 −15 08:00 +10 13:00 −5 17:30 +20 19:30 +10 23:00 −20
Day Mon–Thu 0 Friday +10 Sat/Sun −5
Pickup point CBD +10 Westlands +5 Kilimani 0 Karen +5 Ruaka +10 Embakasi −10
Weather Dry 0 Light rain +5 Heavy rain +15
Traffic news No incidents 0 Any incident +20
Driver rating Any rating 0

Even with all six cards, the trip can still come out up to 5 minutes either way. No card can tell you that part.

generalfeedback.text:
The two most useful cards are usually time of day, which can move the trip anywhere from 20 minutes shorter to 20 minutes longer, and traffic news, which adds 20 minutes when there is an incident. Pickup point and weather come next. Driver rating never changes the trip, so turning it over accounts for none of the variation.

Whatever two cards you choose, the other four are still face down. Their effects are real and knowable, but your prediction leaves them out: that is unaccounted-for variability. The final few minutes either way are natural variability, which no card could predict. This is why a sensible allowance is your prediction plus some spare time.

Your two cards accounted for {@accS@} minutes. The four face-down cards added {@unaccS@} minutes between them. Those are real, known causes of delay, but they weren't in your prediction because you could only see two cards. That is what unaccounted-for variability means: it isn't random, it just hasn't been included. The last {@noiseS@} minutes were natural variability: even with every card turned over, no one could have predicted them.
